result:
**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my stomach like a stone.

I didn’t know then that some sentences are boulders, that they can sit in you for years, pressing against your ribs every time you take a deep breath.

II.

There’s a myth that writers are born with an overflowing well of ideas, that we wake up with sentences already formed on our tongues. The truth is messier. Most days, I sit in front of a blank page and feel like a fraud. The cursor blinks at me, judgmental. *What do you have to say that hasn’t been said before?*

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 chances to build or destroy, to clarify or confuse, to lie or tell the truth. Most of them are forgotten by sunset. But some linger. *"I love you."* *"You’re fired."* *"It’s cancer."* Three words can rewrite a life.

III.

I had a friend in college who believed in the power of unsent letters. She’d stay up all night writing furious, heartbroken, or ecstatic pages to people she’d never speak to again—old lovers, estranged parents, professors who’d failed her. Then she’d burn them in a metal bowl on her fire escape, watching the edges blacken and curl. *"It’s not about them hearing it,"* she’d say. *"It’s about me not carrying it anymore."*

I tried it once. Wrote a letter to my high school bully, the one who called me *"the girl who smells like libraries"* (as if that were an insult). I told him how his words had made me scrub my skin raw in the shower, how I’d stopped reading for pleasure for a year because books became synonymous with shame. I lit the corner of the page and watched the flames lick up the margins. But the weight didn’t lift. Maybe some stones are too heavy to burn away.

IV.

Language is a living thing. It evolves, mutates, dies, and is reborn. Words we use without thinking—*"crazy," "hysterical," "retarded"*—carry the ghosts of their past meanings. We inherit them like hand-me-down clothes, never noticing the stains. I catch myself saying *"that’s so OCD"* about a neatly organized bookshelf, and then I remember my cousin, who can’t leave the house without counting the cracks in the sidewalk in multiples of seven. The weight of my carelessness presses down.

V.

There’s a Japanese word: *komorebi*. It means the sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees. It’s one of those words that makes you realize how much is lost in translation, how English fails to capture the quiet poetry of everyday moments. I think about this when I’m walking in the park and the light spills onto the path in golden patches. How do you explain that kind of beauty to someone who’s never seen it? How do you make them *feel* it?

VI.

I once loved a man who spoke in metaphors. *"You’re like a storm I want to get lost in,"* he’d say, or *"Your silence is a room I can’t find the door to."* It was intoxicating at first, being turned into a landscape, a force of nature. But after a while, I realized he never just said what he meant. Love shouldn’t require a decoder ring.

When I left, he sent me a text: *"You were the only poem I ever memorized."* I didn’t reply. Some words are better left unanswered.

VII.

The heaviest word I know is *"no."* Two letters, one syllable, infinite power. Saying it can feel like pushing against a closed door. *"No, I won’t stay late."* *"No, I don’t want children."* *"No, I’m not okay."* We’re taught that *"no"* is rude, selfish, unkind. But it’s also a boundary, a shield, a declaration of self. The first time I said it without apologizing, I trembled.

VIII.

I work in a coffee shop now, the kind with mismatched mugs and a chalkboard menu that changes daily. Regulars come in and order *"the usual,"* and I already know their drinks, their names, the way they like their oatmeal (extra brown sugar, no nuts). There’s a comfort in the ritual of it. But sometimes, when it’s slow, I watch people through the steam rising from the espresso machine. A couple in the corner, not speaking, both scrolling on their phones. A student with dark circles under her eyes, highlighting a textbook like her life depends on it. An old man who comes in every Tuesday at 3 p.m., orders black coffee, and reads the obituaries.

I wonder what words are sitting in their chests, unsaid.

IX.

My mother used to tell me, *"If you can’t say something nice, don’t say anything at all."* But silence has its own weight. The things we don’t say can crush us just as easily as the things we do. I think about the times I’ve stayed quiet—when a friend made a racist joke, when a partner crossed a line, when I should have told someone I loved them. The absences echo.

X.

I’m running out of words now. 1,000 is more than it seems when you’re staring at a blank page, but less than it feels when you’re trying to hold a life in your hands. Maybe that’s the point. We’re all just trying to distill the chaos into something manageable, to press meaning into these little symbols and hope someone else understands.

Or maybe words are just sounds we make to keep from screaming.

XI.

The last thing my father ever said to me was *"Drive safe."* It was ordinary, throwaway, the kind of phrase that slips out without thought. But it was the last, so now it’s sacred. I repeat it to myself when I’m merging onto the highway, when I’m tired and the yellow lines blur. *"Drive safe."* Two words, a lifetime of weight.

XII.

If I had to choose one word to carry with me forever, it would be *"maybe."* It’s neither yes nor no, neither beginning nor end. It’s the word of possibility, of doors left ajar. It’s the word that keeps me from slamming things shut.

Maybe I’ll write a novel someday.
Maybe I’ll learn to forgive.
Maybe the weight will lift.

Or maybe I’ll just keep carrying it, one word at a time.
